title: Lot and his daughters
source_text: Δέον δ᾿ αὐτὸν τὸ φιλάληθες τῶν ἀναγραψάντων τὰς θείας γραφὰς ἀποδεξάμενον. μὴ κρυψάντων καὶ τὰ ἀπεμφαίνοντα, προσαχθῆναι καὶ περὶ τῶν λοιπῶν καὶ παραδοξοτέρων ὡς οὐ πεπλασμένων, ὁ δὲ τοὐναντίον πεποίηκε καὶ τὰ περὶ τὸν Λὼτ καὶ τὰς θυγατέρας, οὔτε κατὰ τὸ ῥητὸν ἐξετάσας οὔτε κατὰ τὴν ἀναγωγὴν ἐρευνήσας. τῶν Θυεστείων εἶπε κακῶν ἀνομώτερα. τὰ μὲν οὖν τῆς κατὰ τὸν τόπον τροπολογίας οὐκ ἀναγκαῖον νῦν λέγειν, τίνα τε τὰ Σόδομα. καὶ τίς ὁ πρὸς τὸν ἐκεῖθεν διασῳζόμενον τῶν ἀγγέλων λόγος, φασκόντων· „μὴ περιβλέψῃ εἰς τὰ ὀπίσω μηδὲ στῇς ἐν πάσῃ τῇ περιχώρῳ· εἰς τὸ ὄρος σῴζου, μή ποτε συμπαραληφθῇς,“ καὶ τίς ὁ Λὼτ, τίς τε ἡ γυνὴ αὐτοῦ, γενομένη „στήλη ἁλὸς“ διὰ τὸ ἐστράφθαι εἰς τοὐπίσω, καὶ τίνες αἱ θυγατέρες αὐτοῦ, καταμεθύσκουσαι τὸν πατέρα, ἵνα γένωνται ἐξ αὐτοῦ μητέρες· φέρε δὲ τὰ τῆς κατὰ τὴν ἱστορίαν ἀπεμφάσεως δι᾿ ὀλίγων παραμυθησώμεθα, τὴν τῶν ἀγαθῶν καὶ κακῶν καὶ ἀδιαφόρων ἐζήτησαν καὶ Ἕλληνες φύσιν· καὶ οἱ ἐπιτυγχάνοντές γε αὐτῶν τὰ μὲν ἀγαθὰ καὶ κακὰ τίθενται ἐν προαιρέσει μόνῃ, πάντα δὲ ἀδιάφορα τῷ ἰδίῳ λόγῳ φασὶν εἶναι τὰ χωρὶς προαιρέσεως ἐξεταζόμενα· τὴν δὲ προαίρεσιν τούτοις χρωμένην δεόντως μὲν ἐπαινετὴν εἶναι, οὐ δεόντως δὲ ψεκτήν, εἶπον οὖν ἐν τῷ περὶ ἀδιαφόρων τόπῳ ὅτι τῷ ἰδίῳ λόγῳ θυγατράσι μίγνυσθαι ἀδιάφορόν ἐστιν, εἰ καὶ μὴ χρὴ ἐν ταῖς καθεστώσαις πολιτείαις τὸ τοιοῦτον ποιεῖν, καὶ ὑποθέσεως χάριν πρὸς παράστασιν τοῦ ἀδιάφορον εἶναι τὸ τοιοῦτον παρειλήφασι τὸν σοφὸν μετὰ τῆς θυγατρὸς μόνης καταλελειμμένον, παντὸς τοῦ τῶν ἀνθρώπων γένους διεφθαρμένου, καὶ ζητοῦσιν εἰ καθηκόντως ὁ πατὴρ συνελεύσεται τῇ θυγατρὶ ὑπὲρ τοῦ μὴ ἀπολέσθαι κατ᾿ αὐτὴν τὴν ὑπόθεσιν τὸ πᾶν τῶν ἀνθρώπων γένος. ἆρ᾿ οὖν παρὰ μὲν Ἕλλησιν ὑγιῶς ταῦτα λέγεται, καὶ οὐκ εὐκαταφρόνητος αὐτοῖς αἵρεσις ἡ τῶν Στωϊκῶν συναγορεύει· ἐπὰν δὲ κόρια, περὶ ἐκπυρώσεως τοῦ κόσμου μεμαθηκότα οὐ τετρανωκότα δὲ, ἰδόντα πῦρ διειληφὸς τὴν πόλιν αὐτῶν καὶ τὴν χώραν, ὑπολαμβάνοντα ζώπυρον τοῦ γένους τῶν ἀνθρώπων καταλελεῖφθαι ἐν τῷ πατρὶ καὶ αὐταῖς, βουληθῇ διὰ τὴν τοιανδὶ ὑπόληψιν συστήσασθαι τὸν κόσμον, ἐλάττονα ἔσται τοῦ κατὰ τὴν τῶν Στωϊκῶν ὑπόθεσιν σοφοῦ, καθηκόντως ἐν τῇ φθορᾷ τῶν πάντων ἀνθρώπων μιγνυμένου ταῖς θυγατράσιν; οὐκ ἀγνοῶ δ᾿ ὅτι προσκόψαντές τινες τῷ βουλήματι τῶν τοῦ Λὼτ θυγατέρων καὶ ἀνόσιον τὸ ἔργον εἶναι ὑπειλήφασι καὶ ὡς ἐξ ἀνοσίων μίξεων εἰρήκασι γεγονέναι ἔθνη ἐπάρατα, τὸ Μωαβιτῶν καὶ τὸ Ἀμμανιτῶν, καὶ ἀληθῶς γε οὐχ εὑρίσκεται ἡ θεία γραφὴ σαφῶς παραδεξαμένη ὡς καλῶς γεγενημένον τὸ τοιοῦτον ἢ αἰτιασαμένη καὶ μεμψαμένη· πλὴν ὅπως ποτὲ ἔχει τὸ γενόμενον, ἀνάγεται μὲν ἐπὶ τροπολογιαν ἐχει δέ τινα καὶ καθ᾿ αὑτὸ ἀπολογίαν.
pass_a_gloss: It being needful (δέον) that he, having accepted (ἀποδεξάμενον) the truth-loving (φιλάληθες) of those who recorded the divine scriptures, not having hidden even the incongruous/unseemly things (ἀπεμφαίνοντα), be brought (προσαχθῆναι) also concerning the rest and more paradoxical (παραδοξοτέρων) as not fabricated (πεπλασμένων); but he did the opposite, and the things about Lot and the daughters, neither examining according to the letter (κατὰ τὸ ῥητόν) nor searching according to anagogy (κατὰ τὴν ἀναγωγήν), he called more lawless (ἀνομώτερα) than the Thyestean evils (Θυεστείων κακῶν). The tropology of the place it is not necessary now to say, what the Sodom is, and what the word of the angels to the one being saved (διασῳζόμενον) from there, saying: 'do not look around to the things behind, nor stand in all the surrounding country (περιχώρῳ); to the mountain save yourself (σῴζου), lest you be taken along together (συμπαραληφθῇς)', and who Lot is, who his wife, having become 'a pillar (στήλη) of salt' through having turned (ἐστράφθαι) backward, and who his daughters, making the father drunk (καταμεθύσκουσαι) so as to become mothers from him; but come (φέρε), let us in few words soothe (παραμυθησώμεθα) the incongruity (ἀπεμφάσεως) according to the history (ἱστορίαν). The Greeks also sought the nature (φύσιν) of goods and evils and indifferents (ἀδιαφόρων); and those of them succeeding (ἐπιτυγχάνοντες) place goods and evils in the will/choice (προαιρέσει) alone, and say all things examined apart from will are indifferent in their own account (τῷ ἰδίῳ λόγῳ); and the will using these as it ought (δεόντως) is praiseworthy, not as it ought, blameworthy (ψεκτήν). They said then in the topic (τόπῳ) on indifferents that in its own account to have intercourse (μίγνυσθαι) with daughters is indifferent, even if one must not do such in the established polities (καθεστώσαις πολιτείαις), and for hypothesis' sake (ὑποθέσεως χάριν), to present it as indifferent, they took the wise man (σοφόν) left with his daughter alone, the whole race of men having been destroyed (διεφθαρμένου), and they ask whether fittingly/dutifully (καθηκόντως) the father will come together (συνελεύσεται) with the daughter for the sake of the whole race of men not perishing according to this very hypothesis. Then is this soundly (ὑγιῶς) said among Greeks, and the not easily despised school (αἵρεσις) of the Stoics argues for (συναγορεύει) it; but when girls (κόρια), having learned about the conflagration (ἐκπυρώσεως) of the world but not having grasped it clearly (τετρανωκότα), having seen fire overspreading (διειληφός) their city and country, supposing that a spark/live coal (ζώπυρον) of the race of men had been left in the father and themselves, wished through such supposition (ὑπόληψιν) to establish (συστήσασθαι) the world, will they be lesser than the wise man according to the Stoics' hypothesis, fittingly in the destruction (φθορᾷ) of all men having intercourse with the daughters? I am not ignorant that some, having stumbled at (προσκόψαντες) the intent (βουλήματι) of Lot's daughters, have supposed the deed unholy (ἀνόσιον) and have said that from unholy unions came accursed (ἐπάρατα) nations, the Moabites and the Ammonites; and truly the divine scripture is not found clearly having accepted (παραδεξαμένη) such as having happened well, or having charged (αἰτιασαμένη) and blamed (μεμψαμένη) it; however the thing that happened stands, it is referred (ἀνάγεται) to tropology, but it also has in itself a certain defence (ἀπολογίαν).
pass_b_english: He ought to have welcomed the love of truth in those who wrote the divine Scriptures, who did not hide even what is unseemly, and so been led to accept the rest too, even the more marvellous things, as not invented. But he has done the opposite: the story of Lot and his daughters (Genesis 19:30–38), which he neither examined according to the letter nor searched out by its higher sense, he called “more lawless than the crimes of Thyestes.”

Now there is no need to speak at present of the figurative sense of the passage: what Sodom is, and what is meant by the word of the angels to the man escaping from there, when they say, “Do not look behind you, nor stop anywhere in the whole surrounding region; escape to the mountain, lest you too be swept away” (Genesis 19:17); and who Lot is, and who his wife, who became “a pillar of salt” (Genesis 19:26) because she turned back; and who his daughters are, who made their father drunk so as to become mothers by him (Genesis 19:32–36).

But come, let us in a few words ease what seems unseemly in the story taken literally. The Greeks too inquired into the nature of things good, evil and indifferent; and those of them who hit the mark place good and evil in the will alone, and say that all things considered apart from the will are, in their own nature, indifferent, but that the will, when it uses these as it ought, is praiseworthy, and when it does not, blameworthy. So they have said, in their treatment of indifferent things, that in its own nature intercourse with daughters is indifferent, even though one must not do such a thing in established societies. And by way of hypothesis, to show that such a thing is indifferent, they have taken the case of a wise man left alone with his daughter after the whole human race has been destroyed, and they ask whether the father will fittingly come together with his daughter, so that, on that very hypothesis, the whole human race may not perish.

Is this, then, soundly said among the Greeks, with the far from contemptible school of the Stoics arguing for it? And when young girls who have heard of the burning of the world but have not understood it clearly see fire spreading over their city and their land (Genesis 19:24–25), and, supposing that an ember of the human race has been left in their father and themselves (Genesis 19:31), wish on that supposition to found the world again, will they be worse than the wise man of the Stoics’ hypothesis, who fittingly comes together with his daughters when all mankind has perished?

I am not unaware that some, offended at the intention of Lot’s daughters, have judged the deed unholy, and have said that from unholy unions accursed nations were born, the Moabites and the Ammonites (Genesis 19:37–38). And indeed the divine Scripture is not found clearly approving such a deed as well done, nor charging and blaming it. But however the event stands, it is taken up into a figurative sense, and it also has some defence in itself.

choices.term: τὰ τῆς κατὰ τὴν ἱστορίαν ἀπεμφάσεως
choices.choice: τὰ τῆς κατὰ τὴν ἱστορίαν ἀπεμφάσεως: 'relieve the apparent unseemliness of the story' changed to 'ease what seems unseemly in the story taken literally' (κατὰ τὴν ἱστορίαν was lost)
καθηκόντως: 'rightly' changed to 'fittingly' (twice), matching the Stoic καθῆκον noted
Girls' sentence: past tenses ('had heard … saw … wished') changed to the present general case of ἐπὰν + subjunctive, matching the future 'will they be'
ζώπυρον: 'a spark' changed to 'an ember', echoing 'embers of life' in 4.41
Added inline (Genesis 19:24–25) beside the fire over city and land, and to bible_refs
Translator note updated for these choices

Copy-text: staged source_4.json section 45 (Koetschau 4.45). The opening sentence is an awkward accusative-and-infinitive (δέον … προσαχθῆναι); rendered by sense as ‘He ought to have … and so been led’. Celsus’s phrase: τῶν Θυεστείων … κακῶν ἀνομώτερα, ‘more lawless than the crimes of Thyestes’ (Thyestes, in Greek legend, ate his own children unknowingly and lay with his daughter). Genesis 19:17 LXX: ‘μὴ περιβλέψῃς εἰς τὰ ὀπίσω μηδὲ στῇς ἐν πάσῃ τῇ περιχώρῳ· εἰς τὸ ὄρος σῴζου, μήποτε συμπαραλημφθῇς’; Origen has περιβλέψῃ and attributes it to the angels (plural), as the context of Genesis 19:15–17 allows; ‘too’ renders the συμ- of συμπαραληφθῇς. ἀναγωγή is rendered ‘higher sense’, τροπολογία ‘figurative sense’; τὰ τῆς κατὰ τὴν ἱστορίαν ἀπεμφάσεως as ‘what seems unseemly in the story taken literally’. The Stoic terms: ἀδιάφορα ‘indifferent things’, προαίρεσις ‘the will’, καθηκόντως ‘fittingly’ (the Stoic ‘fitting act’, καθῆκον). The Stoic case of the wise man and his daughter after the destruction of mankind is usually filed as a Chrysippus fragment (von Arnim, SVF III), but Origen names no book, so no classical citation is given inline. The girls’ sentence is a general case (ἐπὰν … βουληθῇ … ἔσται), so it is kept in the present with a future main verb. Genesis 19:24–25 (fire on the cities and the surrounding region) is cited beside the fire the daughters saw, and Genesis 19:31 (‘there is no man on the earth’) beside their supposition, as clear allusions. ζώπυρον (‘an ember’) echoes the ζώπυρα of every kind saved in the ark (4.41). ‘Found the world again’ for συστήσασθαι τὸν κόσμον: ‘again’ makes explicit the restoration implied by the burning. ‘Accursed nations’ is the view of ‘some’; Deuteronomy 23:3–4 (Ammonites and Moabites excluded from the assembly) may lie behind it, but Origen does not quote it, so it is not cited inline.
